html:
1What You Will Learn

  • The Claude model families: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus (and the newer top tier)
  • How models differ in capability, speed and cost
  • How to match a model to a task
  • What effort and thinking settings change, and when to raise or lower them

2The Model Families

Running case

Cedarbrook's Reply Queue

  • Customer care sends hundreds of short reply drafts a day
  • Strategy needs a deep analysis of a new market once a quarter
  • Using the most powerful model for the replies wastes time and usage; using a light model for the strategy risks shallow reasoning

Family Positioning (docs) Speed Relative cost Typical business use
Haiku High-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction and routing Fastest Lowest Short reply drafts, sorting tickets, tagging feedback, quick extraction
Sonnet Best combination of speed and intelligence Fast Middle Everyday drafting, analysis, summaries, most daily work
Opus Long-running, demanding knowledge work, more capable Moderate (slower) Higher Complex analysis, long documents, difficult reasoning
Fable (newer top tier) Beyond the guide Demanding reasoning and long-horizon work Slower Highest The hardest problems
  • Every family offers the same basics (text and image input, large context window); they differ in depth of reasoning, speed and cost.
  • Models are released in generations (for example 5.5). Newer versions are generally stronger. Names and numbers change often [Verify live]; the tiering idea (light, balanced, powerful) is what the exam tests.
  • Training knowledge has a cutoff date for every model; current events need web search (Module 3).
  • In the app, open the model picker next to the send button. You can switch model at any point; the change applies from the next response. Admins on Team and Enterprise plans can turn models off for some roles.
Exam tip

Think in three words: Haiku = fast and cheap, Sonnet = balanced, Opus = most capable and slower. The best answer matches the family to the task, not "always the biggest".

3Aligning Model to Task

Task Better fit Why
Hundreds of short replies, tags or categories Haiku Speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning
Everyday drafting, summaries, spreadsheets, meeting notes Sonnet Strong quality at good speed
Complex multi-document analysis, nuanced writing, difficult logic Opus (or the top tier) Depth of reasoning pays off
A first try on a new task type Start with the balanced model, then move up or down Test before committing
  • Start light, step up when needed. If the output is shallow, wrong or ignores constraints even with a clear prompt, try a stronger model. If a task is easy and quality is already fine, a lighter one saves time and usage.
  • Always the biggest model is a trap: it is slower and uses your limit faster. Always the smallest is also a trap: hard reasoning may fail.
  • Try the same prompt on two models for a representative sample and compare quality, speed and usage.
  • Quality, speed and cost are linked. More capable models and higher effort mean slower replies and faster use of your usage limit.
  • Match the model to the stakes, but remember: a stronger model still needs verification (Module 4).
Exam tip

Scenario keywords: "high volume", "short", "simple", "fast", "low cost" point to the light model; "complex", "deep", "nuanced", "long documents" point to the most capable one.

4Effort and Thinking

Besides the model, the app lets you control how hard Claude thinks.

Setting What it does When to use
Effort: low or medium Less thinking; faster; stretches usage Routine tasks
Effort: high Best overall balance of quality and speed Everyday default for many models
Effort: extra high or max More thorough; slower; more usage The hardest analysis and correctness-critical work
Thinking (extended thinking) Claude plans and explores approaches before answering Math, multi-step reasoning, complex planning
  • Effort and thinking are separate settings and can be combined. Some newer models always think, so you lower effort instead of turning thinking off.
  • Higher effort = more thorough but slower and it reaches your usage limit sooner.
  • Defaults suit most tasks. Simple questions and general writing do not need extra effort. Raise it for math and proofs, detailed document analysis, comprehensive plans and multi-step technical problems.
  • Clear prompts matter more than raising effort: a vague prompt at max effort is still vague.
  • The thought summary can be expanded above the answer; you can read how Claude approached the task, but verify the result anyway.

5Cost and Speed in Practice

  • Paid plans have a five-hour session limit and weekly limits; model, effort, conversation length, tools and attachments all affect how fast you use them (Module 16).
  • To stretch usage: use a lighter model or lower effort for routine tasks, turn off thinking where a toggle exists, batch similar requests, and remove tools you do not need.
  • A teamwide pattern works well: a light model for high-volume drafting, the balanced one for daily work, the most capable one reserved for the hard problems.
Exam tip

A vague prompt on a bigger model is still vague: fix the prompt and the setting before paying for more capability.

6Exam Q&A

S1Customer care needs hundreds of short reply drafts a day where speed and cost matter most. Which choice fits best?

  • AA faster, lower-cost model suited to simple, high-volume tasks
  • BThe most capable model for every reply
  • CNo model; write each reply manually
  • DResearch mode for every reply
Show the answer

Answer: A. Light, fast, low-cost models fit high-volume, straightforward work, because fast replies at low cost count for more here than depth of analysis.

S2A strategist must analyze five long reports and produce nuanced recommendations once a quarter. Which choice fits best?

  • AA model chosen at random, because all models perform about the same
  • BThe lightest model with the lowest effort, to keep the cost of the analysis down
  • CA more capable model, possibly with higher effort or thinking
  • DNo model, only web search
Show the answer

Answer: C. Complex, low-volume work with nuanced conclusions justifies the depth of a more capable model, even though it is slower.

S3Which description matches Sonnet?

  • AFastest and lowest cost, for the simplest high-volume tasks
  • BA balanced combination of speed and intelligence for everyday work
  • COnly for image tasks
  • DThe slowest and the most expensive of all the model families that exist
Show the answer

Answer: B. Sonnet sits in the middle: strong, fast, general purpose.

S4A user sets maximum effort for a simple formatting request and the reply is slow and uses much of their limit. What is the best lesson?

  • AMax effort is always better, whatever the task happens to be and however simple
  • BFormatting is not possible
  • CEffort has no effect on usage or on how long the replies take to arrive
  • DSimple tasks do not need extra effort; match effort to the task
Show the answer

Answer: D. Higher effort is slower and consumes more usage; defaults suit routine tasks.

S5Which TWO statements about model selection are correct? Select TWO.

  • ATrying the same prompt on two models can help you decide
  • BThe most capable model is always the right choice
  • CThe right model depends on task complexity, volume, speed and cost
  • DA stronger model removes the need to verify output
  • EModel choice has no effect on speed
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. Matching and testing are the practices; capability never removes verification.

S6A vague prompt gets a weak answer on a light model. What is the best first step?

  • ASwitch to the most expensive model right away, because the model is certainly the cause of the weak result
  • BGive up
  • CImprove the prompt with context, format and constraints, then re-test and step up only if needed
  • DTurn off all features
Show the answer

Answer: C. A clear prompt is often the cheapest improvement; escalate the model if needed.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Haiku Fastest, lowest cost; high-volume, simple, latency-sensitive
Sonnet Balanced speed and intelligence; everyday work
Opus Most capable of the three; slower, higher cost; complex work
Top tier (Fable) Hardest reasoning; slowest, highest cost
Rule Start with the balanced model; step up or down by evidence
Effort Low and medium routine; high balanced; extra high and max for hardest work; higher = slower and more usage
Thinking Plans before answering; separate from effort; some models always think
Trap "Always biggest" and "always smallest"
Always Verify output regardless of model
